source_document: FCA PS22/9 and FCA 2022/31 (PRIN 2A) – extracted marketing-auditable rules
scope_note: This ruleset extracts only those Consumer Duty obligations that can be assessed directly against a specific piece of customer-facing marketing or communication (including web/app content, emails, social posts, in‑app flows, and scripts). It covers: the Consumer Principle where it shapes outcomes evident in communications; cross‑cutting duties (good faith, avoiding foreseeable harm, enabling/supporting objectives) insofar as they manifest in how products are described and how choices are framed; the consumer understanding outcome (PRIN 2A.5); and aspects of consumer support and vulnerability that are visible in how support options and limitations are described in marketing. It deliberately excludes obligations that require evidence of internal processes, governance, testing regimes, monitoring, outsourcing controls, or distribution‑chain role allocation, as these cannot be reliably assessed from the marketing text alone. It also does not restate generic Equality Act or data‑protection duties except where they affect how communications must treat or describe vulnerable customers.

rules.principle: Marketing and customer communications for retail products must act to deliver good outcomes for retail customers, not just promote sales.
rules.check: Does the communication, taken as a whole, appear designed to help the intended retail customers reach good financial outcomes (e.g. by presenting balanced information, risks and limitations) rather than focusing solely on generating sales or uptake?
red_flags: sales-focused language with no explanation of key risks or limitations
headlines promising gains with no balancing information
omitting obvious downsides of a featured product
copy that frames harmful or unsuitable use as normal or desirable

rules.principle: Communications must reflect acting in good faith by being honest, fair, open and consistent with the reasonable expectations created for retail customers.
rules.check: Is the communication honest, fair and open, and does it avoid creating reasonable customer expectations that are contradicted, undermined or quietly limited elsewhere in the same or related material?
red_flags: headline claims contradicted in fine print
benefits heavily promoted while key conditions are buried
using reassuring language while disclosures state the opposite
creating an impression of security or guarantee that legal terms deny

rules.principle: Communications must not be designed to inappropriately manipulate or exploit customers’ emotions, behavioural biases or vulnerabilities to create demand or mislead.
rules.check: Does the communication avoid tactics that obviously exploit fear, urgency, social pressure, complexity or known vulnerabilities to push customers toward a decision that may not be in their interests?
red_flags: “only idiots miss out on this”
“everyone is investing in this right now – don’t be left behind”
countdown timers on complex or long‑term products
messaging that shames customers for not acting immediately
pressure phrases like “you must act in the next few minutes” on high‑risk products

rules.principle: Communications must not take advantage of customers’ characteristics of vulnerability in a way that is likely to cause detriment.
rules.check: Does the communication avoid targeting or wording that appears to exploit people who are likely to be in financial difficulty or otherwise vulnerable (for example by normalising harmful borrowing or minimising consequences for such groups)?
red_flags: “perfect if you’re already struggling with debt”
“no income? no problem”
“ideal if you can’t get credit anywhere else” without clear risk explanation
downplaying repossession or default consequences for high‑risk borrowers
rules.source: PRIN 2A.2.3G(c); PRIN 2A.7.1R–2A.7.5G (needs and characteristics); PS22/9 Ch.10 §10.4–10.7, 10.19–10.20

rules.principle: Communications must not unfairly exploit customers’ behavioural biases, such as inertia or over‑optimism, in ways that are likely to cause foreseeable harm.
rules.check: Does the communication avoid structuring choices or messages in a way that obviously relies on inertia, confusion or over‑optimism to keep customers in disadvantageous products or to take up unsuitable ones?
red_flags: “do nothing and we’ll move you into our default high‑risk plan” without clear warning
auto‑renewal framed as the only easy option while exits are obscured
very complex comparison tables that make the most profitable option look simplest
“you can always cancel later” on products that are actually hard or costly to exit

rules.principle: Communications about products with inherent risks must not imply that the firm will protect customers from those accepted risks or that such risks do not exist.
rules.check: Where a product inherently involves risk (e.g. investment loss, repossession), does the communication avoid implying that customers will not bear these risks or that the firm guarantees to prevent them?
red_flags: “you can’t lose” for investments
“no chance of repossession” on secured lending
“we’ll make sure you never lose money”
omitting any reference to potential loss where it is inherent in the product

rules.principle: Communications must not present or promote unreasonable barriers or additional costs that would foreseeably harm customers who wish to switch, complain, or exit.
rules.check: Does the communication avoid describing or imposing processes, conditions or fees for switching, cancelling or complaining that appear excessive or punitive relative to the product, such that they would foreseeably discourage customers from acting in their interests?
red_flags: high exit fees framed as standard for simple products
“to cancel, you must write to us by post only” where digital onboarding is used
very short or convoluted complaint windows contrasted with easy sign‑up
“if you switch away you will lose all your benefits and pay a penalty” without justification

rules.principle: When a communication acknowledges that customers have suffered harm as a result of the firm’s actions or omissions, it must reflect that the firm will act in good faith and take appropriate remedial action, including redress where appropriate.
rules.check: If the communication admits or refers to past harm caused by the firm, does it also clearly indicate that the firm will take reasonable steps to rectify this, such as explaining remediation, redress, or how affected customers will be supported?
red_flags: acknowledging an error but stating “we accept no responsibility”
“you are solely responsible for any losses from our mistake”
no information on remedy where serious detriment is admitted
language minimising firm fault while denying any support

rules.principle: Communications that encourage customers to pursue particular financial objectives must stay within the firm’s non‑advised or advised remit and not suggest advice where none is given.
rules.check: Where the communication discusses customer goals or suggests courses of action, does it accurately describe whether the service is advisory or non‑advisory and avoid implying personalised advice when only generic information or guidance is provided?
red_flags: “we will tell you exactly what to invest in” for an execution‑only service
using “advice” to describe generic tools or educational content
“personal recommendation” when there is no suitability assessment
small‑print statements of ‘no advice’ that contradict the main messaging

rules.principle: All customer communications, including marketing and post‑sale content, must meet the information needs of the intended retail customers.
rules.check: Does the communication include the key information that a reasonable member of the intended audience would need to understand the product or message and to decide what to do next?
red_flags: no explanation of what the product actually is or does
missing key eligibility or access conditions
omitting material fees or charges from the main description
no indication of what action, if any, the customer should take

rules.principle: Communications must be likely to be understood by the customers intended to receive them, taking account of their characteristics and the product’s complexity.
rules.check: Is the language, structure and overall presentation of the communication such that the intended recipients (given the product and target market) are likely to understand it without specialist knowledge?
red_flags: dense legal or technical wording for mass‑market retail customers
complex jargon without explanation (e.g. “delta‑hedged structured note” in a basic savings ad)
contradictory or circular explanations
overly complex diagrams or tables with no plain‑language summary

rules.principle: Communications must equip retail customers to make decisions that are effective, timely and properly informed.
rules.check: Does the communication present key information and any required actions clearly enough, and early enough, that customers can take or avoid actions in good time based on a proper understanding?
red_flags: critical deadlines buried deep in terms or in small print
“act now” messaging without stating key conditions that affect eligibility or outcomes
sending essential information only after customers are locked in
vague calls to action like “get started” without stating what commitment is involved

rules.principle: Information must be communicated in a way that is clear, fair and not misleading.
rules.check: Does the communication avoid ambiguous, imbalanced or deceptive wording and present information in a way that a reasonable customer would not find misleading?
red_flags: “guaranteed returns” where returns are not guaranteed
“risk‑free” for non‑cash products
headline APR or charges that exclude compulsory fees
graphs or images implying steady growth without noting volatility

rules.principle: Communications must be designed using plain and intelligible language, with any necessary jargon or technical terms clearly explained.
rules.check: Does the communication use everyday language where possible and explain any unavoidable technical or regulatory terms in simple words?
red_flags: extensive use of acronyms without explanation (e.g. “ETF, CFD, ISA, SIPP”)
legal boilerplate pasted into customer‑facing pages
derivatives or leverage terms used without explanation for retail audience
footnotes that are as complex as the main text

rules.principle: Key information in communications must be prominent and easy for customers to identify, using layout and design to support understanding.
rules.check: Are the most important points (such as risks, costs, conditions, customer actions and consequences of inaction) displayed at least as prominently as marketing claims, and easy to spot without reading fine print?
red_flags: risk warnings only in footnotes or in a lighter/ smaller font than benefit claims
placing vital conditions after long scrolls or multiple clicks
colour or design that visually de‑emphasises fees or risks
headline “0% fees” with key exceptions only in dense footnotes

rules.principle: Communications should avoid unnecessary disclaimers that could distract or detract from key information needed for effective decisions.
rules.check: Does the communication avoid excessive, generic or repetitious disclaimers that could obscure or downplay the key information customers need?
red_flags: large blocks of ‘not advice’ text repeated throughout, overwhelming the main message
disclaimers that contradict clear earlier statements rather than clarify them
burying important caveats among long lists of irrelevant warnings
using disclaimers to excuse earlier exaggerated claims

rules.principle: Communications must provide information with an appropriate level of detail, avoiding information overload that prevents effective decision‑making.
rules.check: Is the level of detail in the communication proportionate to the decision and product complexity, without overwhelming customers with unnecessary or poorly structured information?
red_flags: very long undifferentiated text blocks for simple choices
including every possible technical contingency in a sales page instead of layered disclosures
presenting long unstructured fee tables where a short summary plus link would suffice
no use of headings or summaries to break up complex information

rules.principle: Communications must be tailored to the characteristics of the intended retail customers, including any characteristics of vulnerability, and to the product’s complexity and channel used.
rules.check: Does the communication’s content, language and format appear appropriate for the specific target market’s likely financial capability and vulnerabilities, and for the channel (e.g. mobile app, social media, letter) through which it is delivered?
red_flags: complex multi‑step investment explanations squeezed into a small mobile banner
communications for mass‑market products assuming high financial sophistication
no consideration of accessibility for likely vulnerable groups in the target market (e.g. heavy text for visually impaired users without alternatives)
same highly technical content reused across all channels without adaptation

rules.principle: When interacting with customers one‑to‑one, firms must tailor explanations to that individual’s information needs and, where appropriate, check whether they understand and invite questions, especially for key information prompting decisions.
rules.check: Where the material is a script or template for one‑to‑one interactions (e.g. phone scripts, chat flows), does it include prompts to adapt explanations for the customer and to ask if they understand and have questions when key decisions are being discussed?
red_flags: scripts that move straight from explanation to sale without any comprehension check
no allowance to adapt explanations for customers who indicate confusion or vulnerability
instructions to agents to avoid or minimise questions
hard‑sell closers immediately after complex explanations

rules.principle: Where communications are designed to prompt or inform important customer decisions, they should normally be tested in advance (where appropriate) to ensure they support good outcomes.
rules.check: If the communication is clearly intended to drive significant decisions (e.g. product sign‑up, switching, major investments), does it either indicate that it has been tested with customers or at least avoid obvious signs of misunderstanding risk that proper testing would have revealed?
red_flags: decision prompts that are frequently misunderstood in practice but not adjusted (if known from context)
no acknowledgement of complexity or help where decision stakes are high
re‑use of communications known to have caused confusion or complaints
language that conflicts with FAQ or help content

rules.principle: If it becomes apparent from customer behaviour that a communication is not understood or is not delivering good outcomes, the firm must adapt that communication and, where needed, related products or processes.
rules.check: Where the communication itself refers to prior confusion or poor outcomes, does it clearly show that wording, structure or supporting processes have been changed to address those issues?
red_flags: acknowledging that many customers mis‑interpreted earlier messaging without showing any change
keeping identical wording after stating that customers did not understand it
blaming customers for misunderstanding without clarifying the message
no signposting to clearer or updated information after known issues

rules.principle: Firms must avoid using ineffective disclosure as a shield by, for example, hiding critical information in ways customers are unlikely to understand.
rules.check: Does the communication avoid relying on dense or obscure disclosure as the sole means of conveying critical risks, costs or conditions, instead presenting them in a way likely to be genuinely understood?
red_flags: very long T&Cs used as the only place where key risks are stated
“as set out in our terms” without summarising important limitations
placing critical limitations only in downloadable PDFs unlikely to be opened
using complex risk language clearly copied from legal documents without simplification

rules.principle: Communications must make clear when support is limited to certain channels (e.g. digital‑only) so customers can assess if the product meets their needs.
rules.check: If the product or service only provides customer support through limited channels (such as digital‑only), does the marketing clearly state this limitation in a way that is prominent and understandable before sign‑up?
red_flags: promoting a service as convenient without stating it is digital‑only support
mentioning “online self‑service” benefits but hiding that no phone support exists
stating “24/7 support” when it is actually only via FAQs or bots without saying so
support limitations only mentioned deep in FAQs or T&Cs

rules.principle: Where a firm declines access to a product or service, communications should, where appropriate, provide information or signposting to help customers pursue their financial objectives.
rules.check: If the communication is a decline or rejection notice, does it, where appropriate, give constructive next‑step information (such as signposting to guidance, alternative providers or support) rather than simply stating the refusal?
red_flags: bare “application declined” letters with no further information
language implying the customer is uninsurable or ineligible everywhere without basis
no signposting to MoneyHelper or similar where the customer clearly has unmet needs
discouraging customers from seeking other options despite alternatives existing

rules.principle: Where support is primarily or only through one channel (such as digital‑only), marketing must not suggest broader or more flexible support than is actually available.
rules.check: Does the communication avoid implying that customers will receive multi‑channel or personalised support where, in reality, support is restricted (e.g. to self‑service digital tools only)?
red_flags: “we’re always here for you by phone, chat or in person” when only chat exists
suggesting access to ‘experts’ when support is FAQs or bots only
depicting physical branches where the firm is app‑only
“dedicated account manager” claims for standard self‑service tiers
rules.source: PRIN 2A.6.1R; 2A.5.3R(2) (clear, fair, not misleading); PS22/9 Ch.9 §9.6–9.7, 9.56–9.58

rules.principle: Communications must not state or imply that customers cannot reasonably obtain support through a channel that would be needed for common or non‑standard issues (e.g. fraud, access problems).
rules.check: Do product and support descriptions avoid ruling out or discouraging access to any human or real‑time support where it is reasonably foreseeable that some customers will need this for complex or urgent issues?
red_flags: “no phone or live support under any circumstances” for products involving fraud risk or large sums
stating that all issues, including fraud and complaints, must be handled only via email forms
rules that complex changes can only be made via a channel many customers won’t have access to
messages that customers must rely solely on FAQs for all problems

rules.principle: Support‑related communications must reflect that firms will make reasonable adjustments for disabled customers and others with protected characteristics where required by law.
rules.check: Where the communication describes support or access arrangements, does it either mention reasonable adjustments or at least avoid wording that suggests disabled or otherwise protected customers cannot get appropriate adjustments?
red_flags: “we cannot accommodate any special needs or accessibility requests”
“service is only available via voice calls” without any alternative for hearing‑impaired users
statements implying that assistive formats (e.g. large print, braille, screen‑reader compatibility) will not be considered
blanket exclusions of customers based on disability or age without justification

rules.principle: Communications should be designed with the needs of the firm’s actual target market in mind, including customers in vulnerable circumstances, rather than an abstract ‘average’ customer.
rules.check: Does the communication’s content and tone appear to consider the range of likely needs and vulnerabilities in the target market (e.g. lower literacy or numeracy, financial stress) rather than assuming all customers are highly sophisticated and resilient?
red_flags: marketing for sub‑prime or high‑cost products that assumes high financial literacy
no acknowledgment of support for customers in difficulty where the target market is likely to include such customers
language that blames or shames customers in financial hardship
very complex wording for simple retail products aimed at broad audiences

rules.principle: Where the product’s target market is likely to include customers with specific vulnerability drivers (e.g. financial difficulty), communications should signpost relevant support more prominently and accessibly.
rules.check: If the target market clearly includes consumers with common vulnerabilities (such as financial difficulty for sub‑prime credit), does the communication clearly signpost relevant support options or assistance in an accessible way?
red_flags: sub‑prime or high‑risk credit ads with no mention of help if customers struggle to make payments
burying information about support for financial difficulty deep in terms
only providing generic marketing with no signposting to hardship help, despite high‑risk audience
no clear route to contact support for customers in distress

rules.principle: Communications should not suggest that customers in vulnerable circumstances will receive worse outcomes than other customers purely because of their vulnerability.
rules.check: Does the communication avoid indicating that customers will get poorer terms, service or support solely due to disability, age, illness or other vulnerability rather than legitimate risk‑based factors?
red_flags: “we reserve the right to withdraw support if you become ill”
“customers with mental health conditions may not access our full range of services” without lawful justification
blanket exclusions of older or disabled customers presented as convenience for the firm
stating that vulnerable customers must use separate, inferior channels

rules.principle: Where communications refer to diversity, inclusion or protected characteristics, they must be consistent with firms’ obligations under the Equality Act and must not discourage customers who share protected characteristics from engaging.
rules.check: If the marketing mentions or implies anything about gender, ethnicity, disability, age or other protected characteristics, is it framed inclusively and without suggesting that such customers are less welcome or will receive worse treatment?
red_flags: “not suitable for women” or similar gendered exclusion without basis
language implying certain ethnic groups are higher risk and unwelcome
age‑based exclusions stated in disparaging terms (e.g. “we don’t want older customers slowing us down”)
messaging that hints some protected groups will face extra hurdles
